New Rochelle’s COVID-19 Outbreak: A Look Back at the Start of the Pandemic Five years ago, in March 2020, New Rochelle, New York, became the epicenter of the COVID-19 outbreak in the United States, marking a pivotal moment in the nation’s fight against the emerging pandemic. The initial weeks were fraught with uncertainty as details rapidly evolved, and unprecedented measures were implemented to contain the spread of the virus.The events in Westchester County served as a stark reminder of the challenges and anxieties that defined the beginning of the COVID-19 era,setting a precedent for the nation’s response.
The arrival of COVID-19 in New rochelle five years ago feels both recent and distant. Daily news coverage from that period reveals the rapid changes, the limited understanding of the virus, and the lack of established protocols. The experiences in New Rochelle became a model for subsequent actions, including quarantines, mask mandates, contact tracing, and drive-thru testing , all underscored by a pervasive sense of fear.
Looking back at the coverage from the first two weeks of March 2020, as politicians and scientists grappled with policies and prescriptions amid growing worry, can be a difficult experience. The initial phase involved a single case in Manhattan,followed by a lawyer in New Rochelle,his synagogue,and two Rocklanders who catered at a synagogue event. Rumors, fear, a containment zone, and empty store shelves soon followed. People began learning to wash their hands thoroughly, for the duration of a song long enough to kill the virus. Within two weeks, schools were closed, states of emergency were declared, and the world felt significantly smaller.
March 3, 2020: NY Reports First Coronavirus Case March 3, 2020: New York’s first coronavirus case hit the front page. File photo On Monday, March 2, 2020, Gov. Andrew cuomo and New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio addressed concerns about the spread of coronavirus. They stated that the one confirmed case, a 39-year-old Manhattan woman, was well-contained and that the state and city were taking measures to control its spread.
“Her condition is mild. She is at home, and she is not even hospitalized, even though she tested positive for the virus.”
Gov. Andrew Cuomo
At the time, the U.S. death toll reached six, with all deaths occurring in Washington state.
New York Governor Andrew Cuomo and New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio deliver remarks at a news conference regarding the first confirmed case of coronavirus in New York State in Manhattan borough of New York City, New York, U.S.,March 2,2020. andrew kelly, REUTERS March 4, 2020: Westchester COVID Case Confirmed march 4, 2020: A New Rochelle lawyer was confirmed as the first positive COVID case in Westchester. File photo A New Rochelle lawyer tested positive for the coronavirus, despite having no known travel history to countries at the center of the outbreak. This marked a notable shift in the understanding of the virus’s spread within the community.
Westchester County Health Commissioner Sherlita Amler ordered the lawyer’s Young Israel New Rochelle synagogue to halt services. Congregants who attended services on Feb. 22 or a Feb. 23 funeral and bat mitzvah were ordered to quarantine in their homes until at least March 8.
“Those who do not self-quarantine will be mandated by the County Department of Health to do so.”
Dr. sherlita Amler, Westchester Health Commissioner’s order
The U.S. death toll rose to nine.
A New Rochelle lawyer who was diagnosed with coronavirus was admitted to newyork-Presbyterian Lawrence Hospital in Bronxville before being transferred to NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center in Manhattan in March 2020. Seth Harrison/The Journal News Westchester County Executive George Latimer delivers remarks concerning the first case of the Coronavirus Covid-19 in westchester, during a press conference at the westchester County Office Building in White Plains, March 3, 2020. Mark Vergari/The Journal News The events of early March 2020 in New Rochelle serve as a critical reminder of the initial challenges and rapid escalation of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States.The swift implementation of containment measures, though disruptive, provided a framework for subsequent responses across the nation and highlighted the importance of proactive public health strategies in the face of emerging infectious diseases.

Westchester County Schools Shut Down Amid COVID-19 surge, Community on Edge
COVID-19 Cases Surge in Westchester County: Schools Shut, Community on Edge Published: March 6, 2020
Westchester County is facing a rapidly escalating COVID-19 outbreak, leading to school closures and increased anxiety among residents. as of March 6, 2020, the county accounts for a meaningful portion of New York State’s confirmed cases. Eighteen of the state’s 22 cases are located in Westchester, all traced back to a single source: a 50-year-old lawyer from New Rochelle.The situation is quickly evolving,with new cases emerging and precautions intensifying across the region. The initial outbreak and subsequent measures serve as a stark reminder of the pandemic’s early days and the challenges faced in containing the virus.
Dr. Sherlita Amler, Westchester County health commissioner, delivers remarks concerning the first case of the Coronavirus Covid-19 in Westchester, during a press conference at the Westchester County Office Building in White Plains, March 3, 2020. Credit: Mark Vergari/The Journal news March 5,2020: Ten Cases Reported The situation intensified on March 4,2020,when nine additional Westchester County residents tested positive for COVID-19. Authorities confirmed that all nine individuals had direct or indirect contact with the initial Westchester patient. Among the newly infected were the lawyer’s wife and two children, who remain under quarantine in their home located in the Wykagyl section of New Rochelle. This cluster of cases underscores the highly contagious nature of the virus and the challenges in containing its spread within a community. The rapid spread prompted increased testing and contact tracing efforts to mitigate further transmission.
March 5, 2020: nine more positive cases are linked to the New Rochelle lawyer. Credit: File photo The rapid increase in cases has triggered a range of reactions, from heightened awareness to palpable fear. The focus on New Rochelle’s Jewish community,stemming from the initial cluster of cases,has sadly lead to some instances of online backlash,highlighting the potential for stigma and discrimination during a public health crisis. Public health officials emphasized the importance of avoiding stigmatization and focusing on preventative measures to protect all members of the community.
Adding to the community’s concerns, the United Way of Westchester and Putnam’s 2-1-1 helpline has experienced a surge in calls from residents seeking information and guidance related to COVID-19. This influx of inquiries underscores the public’s need for accurate and reliable information during this uncertain time. The helpline provided crucial resources and support to residents navigating the evolving situation.
Nationally, the U.S. death toll from COVID-19 had risen to 11 by this time.In response to the growing threat,both the House and Senate approved an $8 billion emergency funding package aimed at combating the virus and mitigating its impact. The funding package was intended to support vaccine development, testing, and other critical public health initiatives.
It seems like every other house on the block is quarantined. It’s a vrey tight-knit community up here.
Barbara davis, New Rochelle historian, who lives near Young Israel synagogue
Barbara Davis, New Rochelle city historian, lives a few blocks from Young Israel Synagogue, which was the epicenter of the outbreak in the early days of the pandemic. Credit: Seth Harrison/The Journal News New York Gov. Andrew cuomo discusses the new cases of the coronavirus in new Rochelle at a press briefing at the New York Power Authority in White Plains, March 4, 2020. at left is George Latimer, the Westchester County Executive and at right is Howard Zucker, M.D. the NYS Health commissioner and New Rochelle Mayor Noam Bramson.Credit: Mark Vergari/The journal News Young Israel synagogue in New Rochelle in March 4, 2020. Credit: Tania Savayan/The Journal News March 6, 2020: Precautions Increase as Cases Climb By March 6, 2020, the number of confirmed COVID-19 cases in Westchester County had risen to 18, representing the majority of New York’s 22 confirmed COVID cases . The common link among all Westchester cases remained the 50-year-old New Rochelle lawyer.This included a worker from Lawrence hospital in Bronxville, where the lawyer had initially sought treatment, further illustrating the potential for transmission within healthcare settings. Healthcare facilities implemented stricter protocols to protect staff and patients.
March 6, 2020: The cases continue to climb and the first Westchester schools are shut amid COVID concerns. Credit: File photo Growing concerns about potential exposure led to the closure of schools in Hastings-on-Hudson and Mount vernon. This decision left students and parents grappling with uncertainty and anxiety, wondering about their own risk of infection. The school closures highlight the difficult choices facing communities as they attempt to balance public health concerns with the disruption to daily life.Remote learning solutions were explored to minimize the impact on students’ education.
Contact tracing efforts revealed that individuals who had attended synagogue events with the New Rochelle lawyer had traveled to Washington, D.C., to participate in the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) conference. This event, which drew thousands of attendees, raised concerns about potential widespread exposure and further transmission of the virus.Public health officials worked to identify and contact individuals who may have been exposed at the conference.

New Rochelle under Containment as New York COVID-19 Cases Surge
New Rochelle Under “containment Area” as New York Leads Nation in COVID-19 Cases New York is now at the forefront of the nation’s COVID-19 outbreak, prompting governor Andrew Cuomo to take decisive action in New Rochelle. On March 11, 2020, Cuomo announced the deployment of the National Guard to establish a “containment area” around the Young Israel synagogue, the epicenter of a local cluster. This action follows a significant spike in positive cases, with New York reporting 142 cases on monday, March 9, 2020, surpassing Washington state’s count of 105. The “containment area,” effective immediately,encompasses a one-mile radius around the synagogue,impacting schools,religious institutions,and daily life for thousands of residents.
march 11, 2020: Gov. Andrew Cuomo sets “containment area” around New Rochelle synagogue, deploys national Guard.File photo The “containment area” encompasses a one-mile radius around the Young Israel synagogue. Within this zone, schools, houses of worship, and large gathering places will be closed through March 25. The closures include New Rochelle High School, Albert Leonard Middle School, Ward Elementary School, Tuckahoe middle and high schools, and William Cottle School in Eastchester.
National Guard Deployed to Assist Residents The National Guard’s presence in New Rochelle is primarily for logistical support.They are responsible for delivering food to approximately 1,000 residents under precautionary quarantine and assisting with the cleaning of public spaces. Despite the “containment area” designation, there are no checkpoints restricting entry or exit for people or vehicles.
While grocery stores remain open, reports indicate that shelves have been largely cleared of cleaning supplies, and toilet paper has become a scarce commodity. The situation underscores the public’s heightened concern and the rush to secure essential supplies.
School Closures and Educational Continuity The decision to close schools has sparked debate and concern among parents and educators. New Rochelle Superintendent Laura Feijoo addressed parents in an email, stating:
We must make these two weeks count instructionally and ensure students are learning and engaged while we deal with this worldwide crisis.
Laura Feijoo, New Rochelle Superintendent
This suggests a focus on remote learning and maintaining educational continuity during the closure.
New Rochelle schools Superintendent Laura Feijoo and school board President Amy Moselhi discuss possibility of extended school closing raised by the governor, march 9, 2020. Tania Savayan/The Journal News However, the decision to close only select schools has drawn criticism. Martin Daly,of New Rochelle Federation of United School Employees,questioned the logic,stating that:
The decision makes no sense,and anyone familiar with the school district should know that.
Martin Daly,New Rochelle Federation of united School Employees
daly highlighted the fact that siblings from closed schools would still attend other schools within the district,potentially undermining the containment efforts.
Adding to the complexity, New Rochelle Board of Education President Amy moselhi emphasized the importance of keeping schools open unless directed otherwise by authorities.
unless we get a written confirmation from a governing body that has the authority to (close schools), we believe that having students in school is of paramount importance.Putting students at home puts 11,000 students, we consider, at risk.
Amy Moselhi, New Rochelle Board of Education President
Rockland County Cases and regional Impact The impact of the outbreak extends beyond New Rochelle. Rockland County has confirmed six cases, all within Ramapo. As a result, Ramapo High School, Pomona Middle School, and Hempstead Elementary School have also been closed.These cases have been linked to a late February bat mitzvah at Young Israel synagogue in New Rochelle.
Rockland County Executive Ruppert noted that the county’s first cases, involving two catering workers,
“were not forthcoming” about their work locations after exposure in New Rochelle, complicating initial containment efforts.
Statewide Measures and Public Health Response In response to the growing demand for hand sanitizer, Governor Cuomo announced that the state would utilize prison labor to produce it. This initiative aims to address the shortage and provide essential supplies to combat the spread of the virus. The state’s proactive measures reflect the urgency and scale of the public health crisis.
rockland County confirms First Cases On March 7, 2020, Rockland County reported its first two confirmed cases of COVID-19.The individuals, a man and a woman, had attended a bat mitzvah in New Rochelle that was also attended by the 50-year-old New Rochelle attorney who was among the early confirmed cases. Contact tracing efforts are underway, leading to the quarantining of 22 residents after officials retraced the steps of Rockland’s two positive cases, alerting residents who might have visited two Monsey addresses.
March 7, 2020: A man and a woman, caterers at a New rochelle bat mitzvah, are the first in Rockland county to test positive for the coronavirus.Credit: File photo Statewide Response and Growing Concerns The declaration of a state health emergency by Gov. Cuomo on March 8,2020,came as the number of confirmed cases in New York reached 76. By March 9, 2020, the number had climbed to 105.The geographic distribution of cases is as follows: Westchester, 82; NYC, 12; Nassau, 5; Rockland, 2; Saratoga, 2; Suffolk, 1; and Ulster, 1. This rapid increase prompted Cuomo to request federal authorization for private labs to conduct testing, aiming to expand testing capacity and accelerate the identification of new cases.
March 8,2020: Cuomo declares health emergency; 76 cases in NY.Credit: File photo The situation in New Rochelle is especially concerning, leading to targeted interventions. Gov. Cuomo stated that the state is considering closing schools in New Rochelle. additionally, he has implemented a ban on outside visitors to nursing homes and senior living facilities in the area, recognizing the heightened vulnerability of these populations.
“The nursing homes are the most problematic settings for us with this disease,”
Gov. andrew Cuomo
Gov. Andrew Cuomo in a noon briefing march 7, 2020, confirmed additional cases of novel coronavirus including 2 cases upstate in Saratoga County, bringing the statewide total to 76 confirmed cases in New York. Credit: Darren McGee- Office of Governor, Darren McGee- Office of Governor Impact on Schools and Daily Life The escalating outbreak is also impacting schools. On March 6, 2020, John F. Kennedy Elementary School in port Chester sent students and staff home after learning that a family of two students may have had close contact with an infected individual. The possibility of extended school closures is looming, with potential shutdowns lasting for weeks, starting March 10, 2020.
March 9,2020: one week in,105 New York cases.Credit: File photo Despite the growing concerns, some businesses in New Rochelle reported that they had not yet experienced a significant decline in customer traffic as of March 8, 2020.
“It’s still business as usual,”
Nick Triscari at The Wooden Spoon on Division Street
“Hopefully, we do not see a decline in business and people aren’t afraid to leave their house.”
Public Health Recommendations Health officials are urging residents to take precautions to prevent the spread of the virus. Dr. Howard Zucker, New York’s health commissioner, emphasized the importance of basic hygiene practices, stating that both the young and old should
“Wash your hands, continue to stay home if you’re sick and sneeze or cough into your sleeve. They sound boring, but they’
New Rochelle Faces Crisis: schools Shut Down, National Guard Deployed Amid Rising COVID-19 Cases NEW ROCHELLE, N.Y. – As of March 12,2020,New York state was grappling with a surge in COVID-19 cases,prompting decisive action from Governor Andrew cuomo. The state sought federal approval to contract with private labs to significantly increase testing capabilities as confirmed cases reached 212. In a move to curb the spread, officials announced the closure of all State University of New York (SUNY) and city University of New York (CUNY) campuses the following week, a measure impacting higher education statewide. The situation intensified, leading to the deployment of the National Guard and the establishment of containment zones.
Students mill about in front of new Rochelle High School,after dismissal,March 10,2020. Credit: Mark Vergari/The Journal news Business Impact in New Rochelle The Wykagyl section of New Rochelle felt the economic sting as businesses experienced a sharp decline. Coffee shops and restaurants saw a significant drop in customers as residents avoided public areas. Frank Miceli, owner of Minuteman Press, described the situation as dire:
People are staying away from this area. it’s the busiest time of the year for me, but events are being canceled. It’s killing us. We’ll never recoup this money.
The cancellation of events,typically a boon for his business,dealt a severe blow to Minuteman Press and other local establishments,highlighting the economic fallout of the health crisis.
Giovanni Argentari, a custodian with Metro-North Railroad, disinfects public areas at the New Rochelle Metro-North train station, March 10, 2020. Credit: Mark Vergari/The journal News Community Adapts: Purim Celebrated Online Despite the challenges, the community found innovative ways to maintain traditions and connections. Young Israel, such as, held a Purim party online, allowing members to observe the holiday while adhering to precautionary quarantine measures.Purple New Rochelle ribbons were displayed on trees throughout the area, symbolizing solidarity and resilience.
Schools Prepare for Online Learning As schools statewide prepared for a shift to online learning, disparities in resources became apparent across different districts. The transition to remote education highlighted the digital divide and the challenges of ensuring equitable access to learning opportunities for all students.
A mother’s Concerns The school closures presented significant challenges for families, particularly single parents. Annie Rubio, a single mother of four, faced the daunting task of managing three children home from closed schools while her youngest attended a school that remained open. She expressed her anxieties:
As a mom, I’m freaking out. Two weeks is two weeks with four kids. it’s a lot. Teenagers eat like every hour, so here I am at the supermarket.I was just praying that the supermarket was open.
Her concerns reflected the broader anxieties of parents navigating the unprecedented disruption to daily life.
WHO Declares Pandemic On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) officially declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic, underscoring the global scale and severity of the crisis.
New rochelle Schools to Close On March 13, 2020, New Rochelle Superintendent Laura Feijoo announced that all 10 New Rochelle schools would be closed from March 13 through March 25. This decision expanded upon a state order that initially targeted only three schools. Feijoo stated:
I have determined that the closure of all of our schools is the best course of action at this time. … This decision will provide the appropriate federal, state and local authorities the time to develop the best short- and long-term plan for the district.
Laura feijoo, New Rochelle Superintendent
March 13: New rochelle shuts all 10 schools. Credit: File photo National guard Deployed In response to the escalating situation, members of the National Guard were deployed to New Rochelle to assist with food distribution and the cleaning of public spaces. Glen Island Park was repurposed as a COVID-19 testing site, reflecting the community’s efforts to contain the spread of the virus.
#NewRoStrong: Community Solidarity The New Rochelle community rallied together, adopting the hashtag #NewRoStrong to coordinate support for quarantining members of Young Israel. Google Docs were used to track food and other essential items donated to those in need, showcasing the community’s resilience and solidarity.
Impact Beyond New Rochelle The impact of the pandemic extended beyond New Rochelle, with Rockland County reporting a total of seven confirmed cases and the state tallying 328 cases. Metro-North ridership plummeted by 48% on March 12 compared to the previous year, reflecting widespread concerns about public transportation.
Arts and Entertainment Disrupted The arts and entertainment industry also faced significant disruptions. Broadway theaters were closed by state order, with the Broadway League hoping to resume performances by April 13. Pearl river canceled its St. Patrick’s Day Parade, joining other major cities in suspending large public gatherings.
Sports Seasons Suspended The sports world came to a standstill as the NHL suspended its season and high school governing bodies shut down winter championships and all winter sports. High school musicals at Blind Brook and Pleasantville High Schools were among the many performances postponed just hours before their opening nights.
Testing Guidelines New York established specific criteria for COVID-19 testing, prioritizing individuals who had close contact with a confirmed case, traveled to a COVID-19 affected area and exhibited symptoms, were quarantined and showed symptoms, or displayed symptoms and tested negative for other viruses.
National Closures The White House and the U.S. Capitol were closed to tours, further illustrating the widespread impact of the pandemic on daily life and public institutions.
North Avenue in the northern part of New Rochelle known as Wykagyl was deserted was the epicenter of the spread of the Covid-19 virus after congregants of a neighborhood synagogue were the first to be diagnosed with the virus. Credit: Seth Harrison/The Journal News First Drive-Thru Testing Site Opens, State Records First Deaths As the crisis deepened, efforts to expand testing capacity intensified. On March 14,2020,a drive-thru COVID testing facility opened at Glen Island,marking a significant step in increasing testing access. The same week, on March 15, 2020, New York State reported its first deaths attributed to the virus: an 82-year-old New york City woman and a 64-year-old man with pre-existing conditions in rockland County.
Additionally, to combat shortages, the state mobilized resources to produce hand sanitizer. Labor was directed to produce 100,000 gallons of hand sanitizer, branded as “NYS Clean,” to address the shortage of hand sanitizer available to consumers.
Metro-North also took precautions by disinfecting its rail cars, turnstiles, handrails, and ticket vending machines to minimize potential transmission on public transportation. Rockland Sheriff Louis Falco suspended jail visitation and implemented stricter screening procedures for inmates and delivery personnel.
Governor Cuomo emphasized the severity of the situation in New Rochelle, stating:
New Rochelle is a particular problem. It is what they call a cluster.
The implementation of the “containment area” and the deployment of the National Guard reflect the state’s commitment to containing the spread of the virus and protecting public health.
Conclusion The events of March 2020 painted a stark picture of the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in New Rochelle and New York State. From school closures and business disruptions to community solidarity and widespread anxieties,the region faced unprecedented challenges as it navigated the rapidly evolving health crisis. The deployment of the National Guard and the implementation of widespread testing efforts underscored the seriousness of the situation and the collective effort to contain the spread of the virus. The coming days would be crucial in assessing the effectiveness of these interventions and determining the next steps in managing this evolving public health crisis.

New Rochelle Emerges as Epicenter: Drive-Thru Testing and First COVID-19 Deaths in New York State
New Rochelle Emerges as Epicenter: Drive-Thru Testing and First COVID-19 Deaths in new York State In March 2020, New Rochelle, New York, became a focal point in the burgeoning COVID-19 pandemic. The city grappled with a rapid increase in cases, prompting unprecedented measures to contain the spread.The opening of the first drive-thru COVID-19 testing facility on the East Coast at Glen Island Park on March 14, 2020, and the grim milestone of the first COVID-19 deaths in New York State on march 15, 2020, underscored the severity of the escalating health crisis. These events highlighted the urgent need for a coordinated response as communities faced the emerging threat.
March 14,2020: Glen Island Park becomes a drive-thru COVID test facility. (File photo) Drive-Thru Testing Facility Opens at Glen Island on March 14, 2020, Glen Island Park in New Rochelle transformed into the first drive-thru COVID-19 testing facility on the East Coast.This initiative aimed to expedite the testing process and minimize potential exposure risks. The testing site operated by appointment only, prioritizing residents of New Rochelle, although all residents of Westchester County were eligible for testing. The establishment of this facility marked a significant step in the state’s efforts to manage the growing crisis.
Gov. Andrew Cuomo emphasized the importance of this innovative approach, highlighting its efficiency and safety. He stated:
It’s not only faster and easier, it’s also smarter and safer because you’re not exposing people to someone who may be positive. Up until now, you walk into a hospital.
Gov. Andrew Cuomo
New York Governor Andrew Cuomo gets a briefing at glen Island Park in new Rochelle, March 13, 2020. (Mark Vergari/The journal News) First COVID-19 Deaths Reported in New York State The following day, March 15, 2020, brought somber news as New York State reported its first fatalities related to COVID-19. An 82-year-old woman from New york City and a 64-year-old resident of Suffern succumbed to the virus.This marked a grim turning point, bringing the pandemic’s deadly potential into sharp focus. At this point,the total number of confirmed cases in New York had reached 524,underscoring the rapid spread of the virus.
March 15,2020: The headline read,”How did we get here?” over an image of empty store shelves. (File photo) Other Developments Across the Region As the situation unfolded in New Rochelle and across New York state, other counties implemented proactive measures. Putnam County Executive MaryEllen Odell issued a five-day state of emergency order, effective March 16, suspending all classroom and extra-curricular activities for all schools within the county. Rockland County,with its positive cases rising to 9,also moved to establish a drive-thru testing facility at Anthony Wayne Recreation Area.
Statewide, measures were implemented to mitigate the spread of the virus. Most jury trials were postponed to reduce crowding in courtrooms.Gov. Cuomo secured federal approval to utilize both public and private labs for COVID-19 testing, expanding the state’s testing capacity. Additionally,educators proposed the cancellation of annual state tests as schools considered closures.
On the national level, President Donald Trump declared the pandemic a national emergency on March 13, freeing up federal funds and resources to combat the crisis. officials also noted that the pandemic posed a significant challenge to the 2020 Census.
Hospital Bed Capacity and Supply Shortages State officials expressed concern about the availability of hospital beds, with approximately 19,000 out of 53,000 beds currently unfilled. The state also had slightly more than 3,000 intensive-care beds. The looming possibility of a bed shortage added to the urgency of implementing measures to control the spread of the virus.
Across the region, store shelves were rapidly emptied of essential supplies such as cleaning products and toilet paper. Metro-North commuter trains, typically bustling with passengers, were also notably empty, reflecting the growing impact of the pandemic on daily life.
New York Hospitals Postpone Elective Surgeries, Schools Shutter as COVID-19 Spreads As the COVID-19 outbreak intensified in March 2020, New York-Presbyterian Hospital announced the postponement of all elective surgeries. This decision came as spain went into lockdown and several European countries began closing their borders, signaling the growing global concern. The NCAA also canceled its March madness basketball tournament, reflecting the widespread impact of the escalating health crisis. The situation prompted swift action across New York State, with health officials working to trace contacts and contain the spread.
The rapid spread of COVID-19 in early March 2020 triggered a series of unprecedented measures across New York, particularly in Westchester and Rockland counties. The initial detection of the virus in a 50-year-old lawyer from New Rochelle set off a chain reaction, leading to school closures, emergency declarations, and significant disruptions to daily life.
Westchester Schools to Close On March 16, 2020, it was announced that the 44 school districts in Westchester county would close for two weeks. This decision followed similar announcements from New York City, Nassau, and Suffolk counties, highlighting the coordinated effort to mitigate the spread of the virus among students and staff. The closures were scheduled to begin two days after New York City’s, Nassau’s, and Suffolk’s closures.
Adding to the urgency, Gov. Cuomo called on the U.S. Army corps of Engineers to transform buildings across New York into makeshift hospitals, anticipating a surge in patients requiring medical care.
states of emergency Declared March 16, 2020, also saw Westchester County Executive George Latimer and Rockland County Executive Ed Day declare states of emergency for their respective counties. This action granted local authorities greater flexibility in responding to the crisis and implementing necessary measures to protect public health.
Reflecting on the rapidly changing situation, Journal News Executive Editor Mary Dolan described March 16 as “the first day of our new normal, a Monday that ushers in a week with no school, remote work, growing financial uncertainty, disrupted routines and more unrelenting stress.”
The following day, March 17, 2020, the states of emergency in Westchester and Rockland led to the closure of public and private schools, starting March 17 in Rockland and March 18 in Westchester. this marked a significant turning point, just two weeks after the initial case was identified in New Rochelle.
New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut took coordinated action, closing casinos, gyms , cinemas , and theaters. Bars and restaurants were limited to delivery and takeout services,and public gatherings of 50 or more people were paused. The three states also urged residents to stay home and avoid non-essential travel.
New Rochelle Mayor Noam Bramson criticized some companies for declining to deliver to the city, citing its cluster of COVID-19 cases. “It’s a public health hazard,” Bramson stated. “If we’re encouraging people to stay home and engage in social distancing then being able to receive home deliveries is a vital part of that strategy.”
Across New York,more than 80% of public schools had closed or were planning to close,leaving parents scrambling to find childcare and,in some cases,food.food distribution programs were initiated in New Rochelle and Peekskill, with Yonkers scheduled to begin on march 19.
“We have been working very closely with and in support of the actions taken by New York State. However, the time has come that we must take additional actions locally to protect the health and safety of everyone in Rockland.”
Ed Day, Rockland County executive
“When there is any new case you start to do the epidemiological investigation to try to sort it out. and when you start doing that, you start to see that there’s a lot of contacts. Your antennas go up and you start to figure out: ‘OK, what else do we need to do?’”
Dr. Howard Zucker,NYS health commissioner
“We’re all very much aware that we’re facing something that we’ve never faced before.We’re going through a test the likes of which we have not experienced in our adult lifetime here in this country and we’re trying to make decisions as we go along to the best of our ability.”
george Latimer, Westchester County executive

New Rochelle’s Early Battle: A Model for Pandemic Response Published January 1, 2024
Widespread fear and anxiety gripped the community of New Rochelle as it found itself at the forefront of an emerging infectious disease outbreak. The rapid spread and initial uncertainty surrounding the virus presented unprecedented challenges, thrusting the city into the national spotlight. New Rochelle’s experience, though, would become a crucial learning ground, shaping future containment strategies and highlighting the importance of rapid response and community cooperation.
The initial days of the outbreak were marked by a palpable sense of unease. The speed with which the virus spread, coupled with a lack of comprehensive understanding, fueled anxieties among residents. This period underscored the critical need for clear communication and decisive action in the face of an emerging public health crisis.
In response to the escalating situation, New Rochelle implemented a series of measures aimed at containing the spread of the virus. These strategies, including quarantines, contact tracing, and drive-thru testing, were instrumental in slowing the transmission rate and providing valuable data for public health officials.The effectiveness of these early interventions led to their adoption as standard practices in other communities across the nation.
The implementation of drive-thru testing, in particular, proved to be a game-changer. This innovative approach allowed for the rapid and efficient testing of a large number of individuals, enabling health officials to identify and isolate infected individuals more quickly. This proactive measure played a significant role in mitigating the spread of the virus within the community.
The events in New Rochelle highlighted several key lessons regarding the management of infectious disease outbreaks. These included the challenges of containing a rapidly spreading virus, the initial lack of understanding surrounding the virus’s behavior, and the paramount importance of a swift and coordinated response.
